title: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
text:
Hypertrophy of the pyloric circular muscle develops at 2 to 8 weeks of age (peak 3 to 6), most often in first-born boys, with a family history and after early macrolide exposure. Vomiting becomes forceful and projectile, NON-bilious (the obstruction is proximal to the ampulla), after every feed, and the baby remains hungry. A test feed may reveal visible left-to-right gastric peristalsis and an olive-sized mass in the right upper quadrant.
Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid causes hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; the kidney conserves sodium at the cost of hydrogen ions, giving a paradoxical aciduria. Ultrasound confirms a thickened (over about 3 mm), elongated pylorus. The metabolic derangement must be corrected with IV fluids BEFORE surgery (alkalosis depresses breathing after anaesthesia); Ramstedt pyloromyotomy splits the muscle down to the mucosa and cures it.

title: Hirschsprung disease
text:
Neural crest cells migrate down the gut from cranial to caudal to form the myenteric and submucosal plexuses. If migration stops early, the distal bowel is aganglionic and cannot relax, causing functional obstruction; it always involves the rectum and extends proximally, confined to the rectosigmoid in about three-quarters of cases. It is commoner in boys, in Down syndrome and with RET mutations.
Neonates fail to pass meconium within 48 hours and develop abdominal distension and bilious vomiting; rectal examination may cause an explosive release of stool and gas. Older children have chronic severe constipation from birth with failure to thrive. Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis (fever, foul diarrhoea, distension) is the life-threatening complication. Contrast enema shows a narrow distal segment with dilated bowel above (transition zone); rectal suction biopsy is diagnostic (no ganglion cells, increased acetylcholinesterase-positive nerve fibres). Treatment is resection of the aganglionic segment with a pull-through of normal bowel.

title: Malrotation and midgut volvulus
text:
During weeks 6 to 10 the midgut herniates into the umbilical cord, rotates 270 degrees anticlockwise around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery and returns, fixing the duodenojejunal flexure to the left of the spine and the caecum in the right iliac fossa, so the mesentery has a long, broad base. In malrotation the base is narrow and peritoneal (Ladd) bands run from the malpositioned caecum across the duodenum.
The narrow mesentery can twist (midgut volvulus), strangulating the whole midgut. BILIOUS VOMITING IN A NEONATE is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise, a surgical emergency because the entire small bowel can die within hours. An upper gastrointestinal contrast study shows the duodenojejunal flexure to the right of the midline or a 'corkscrew' duodenum; ultrasound may show the superior mesenteric vein lying to the LEFT of the artery (reversed) and a 'whirlpool' sign. The Ladd procedure untwists the bowel, divides the bands, widens the mesentery and removes the appendix.

title: Intussusception
text:
One segment of bowel telescopes into the next, most often the terminal ileum into the caecum (ileocolic). The peak age is 6 to 18 months, when the lead point is usually hypertrophied lymphoid tissue (Peyer patches and mesenteric nodes) after a viral infection. In older children and adults a pathological lead point is more likely: Meckel diverticulum, polyp, lymphoma or Henoch-Schönlein purpura.
The child has episodes of inconsolable crying with pallor and drawing up of the legs, separated by lethargy, then vomiting; 'redcurrant jelly' stool (blood and mucus from venous congestion) and a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant are late signs. Ultrasound shows a target or doughnut sign. After resuscitation, most are reduced by air (pneumatic) enema under fluoroscopy; peritonitis or failed reduction requires surgery. Mesenteric venous congestion progresses to arterial ischaemia and perforation if diagnosis is delayed.

title: Biliary atresia and choledochal cyst
text:
Any term baby still jaundiced after 14 days (21 in preterm babies) needs a split bilirubin. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with pale, acholic stools and dark urine suggests biliary atresia, a progressive fibro-obliterative destruction of the extrahepatic bile ducts that leads to cirrhosis. Ultrasound may show an absent or small gallbladder, and a HIDA scan shows no excretion into the gut. The Kasai portoenterostomy, joining a Roux loop of jejunum to the porta hepatis, works best before about 60 days of age; biliary atresia remains the commonest indication for liver transplantation in children.
A choledochal cyst is a congenital dilatation of the bile ducts, most often fusiform dilatation of the common bile duct (Todani type I), associated with an abnormal pancreaticobiliary junction. It presents with abdominal pain, jaundice and a mass, cholangitis or pancreatitis. Because of a high risk of cholangiocarcinoma, the cyst is excised and bile drainage restored by hepaticojejunostomy.

title: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula
text:
The tracheo-oesophageal septum divides the foregut into the trachea in front and the oesophagus behind in week 4; incomplete division produces atresia with or without a fistula. The commonest type (about 85%) is a blind upper oesophageal pouch with a distal fistula between the trachea and lower oesophagus.
Antenatal polyhydramnios (the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid) is a clue. After birth the baby froths saliva, chokes, coughs and becomes cyanosed with feeds, risking aspiration pneumonitis. A nasogastric tube will not pass and coils in the upper pouch on radiograph; gas in the stomach shows that a distal fistula is present. Associated anomalies are common (VACTERL: vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal and limb defects). Treatment is fistula ligation and primary anastomosis; later problems include anastomotic stricture, reflux and tracheomalacia. An isolated 'H-type' fistula without atresia presents later with choking and recurrent pneumonia.

title: Cleft lip and palate, and Pierre Robin sequence
text:
Cleft lip results from failure of the maxillary prominence to fuse with the medial nasal prominences (intermaxillary segment) in weeks 4 to 7, so the cleft lies lateral to the philtrum, unilateral or bilateral, and may continue through the alveolus to the incisive foramen. Cleft palate results from failure of the lateral palatine shelves to fuse with each other and the nasal septum in weeks 7 to 10, behind the incisive foramen. Risk factors include family history, maternal smoking, antiepileptic drugs (phenytoin, valproate) and folate deficiency; many are syndromic (22q11 deletion).
Consequences: feeding difficulty (special bottles), otitis media with effusion because tensor veli palatini cannot open the auditory tube (grommets are often needed), hypernasal speech from velopharyngeal insufficiency and dental problems. The lip is usually repaired around 3 months and the palate at 6 to 12 months. A bifid uvula with a notched hard palate indicates a submucous cleft.
Pierre Robin sequence: micrognathia displaces the tongue backwards (glossoptosis), obstructing palatal closure (a U-shaped cleft) and the airway; babies are nursed prone or need a nasopharyngeal airway.

title: Branchial cleft cysts, sinuses and fistulas
text:
Second arch anomalies are by far the commonest. A branchial cyst presents in young adults as a smooth, fluctuant swelling at the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid at the junction of its upper and middle thirds, often enlarging or becoming infected after an upper respiratory infection; aspirate contains cholesterol crystals. A second arch sinus or fistula opens on the skin along the lower anterior border of sternocleidomastoid and tracks upward between the internal and external carotid arteries, above the hypoglossal and glossopharyngeal nerves, to the tonsillar fossa, the remnant of the second pouch.
First arch anomalies lie near the ear, angle of the mandible or parotid and are intimately related to the facial nerve. Third and fourth arch sinuses arise from the piriform fossa and present as recurrent left-sided neck abscesses or suppurative thyroiditis.
In an adult over 40, a 'branchial cyst' is a cystic metastasis (often HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer or thyroid papillary carcinoma) until proven otherwise.

title: First pharyngeal arch syndromes: Treacher Collins and hemifacial microsomia
text:
The first pharyngeal arch forms the maxilla, zygoma, mandible (around Meckel's cartilage), the malleus and incus and the muscles of mastication (trigeminal nerve); the second arch forms the stapes, styloid process and muscles of facial expression (facial nerve). Neural crest defects in the first arch therefore affect the face, jaw and middle ear together.
Treacher Collins syndrome (autosomal dominant, TCOF1): bilateral hypoplasia of the zygomatic bones and mandible, downslanting palpebral fissures, notched lower eyelids (colobomas), small malformed ears and conductive deafness from ossicular malformation, with normal intelligence. Airway obstruction and feeding problems need attention in infancy, and hearing aids are fitted early.
Hemifacial microsomia is the unilateral, sporadic counterpart, with a small mandible and ear on one side, sometimes with facial nerve palsy. Pierre Robin sequence and DiGeorge syndrome (third and fourth pouches) are other arch-related conditions.

title: Congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot)
text:
Structural clubfoot affects about 1 in 1000 births, boys twice as often, and is bilateral in half. The deformity is remembered as CAVE: midfoot Cavus, forefoot Adductus, hindfoot Varus and Equinus, with medial displacement of the navicular on the talar head and tight tibialis posterior, calcaneal tendon and medial soft tissues. Unlike positional talipes from intrauterine moulding, it cannot be corrected passively to neutral.
It may be idiopathic or associated with neuromuscular conditions (spina bifida, arthrogryposis), so the spine, hips (developmental dysplasia) and neurology must be examined. The Ponseti method corrects it with weekly manipulations and long-leg casts, usually followed by a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy to correct the equinus, then a foot abduction brace worn at night until about four years of age; non-compliance with the brace is the main cause of relapse. Extensive surgical release is now rarely needed.

title: Fontanelles and craniosynostosis
text:
The posterior fontanelle closes by about 2 months and the anterior fontanelle by 12 to 18 months. A bulging anterior fontanelle in a quiet baby indicates raised intracranial pressure (meningitis, hydrocephalus, haemorrhage); a sunken one indicates dehydration. Delayed closure suggests hypothyroidism, rickets or raised pressure.
Craniosynostosis is premature fusion of a suture, so the skull cannot grow perpendicular to it and expands parallel to it. Sagittal synostosis is commonest, producing a long narrow skull (scaphocephaly); unilateral coronal gives anterior plagiocephaly with a raised orbit ('harlequin eye' on radiographs); metopic gives a triangular forehead (trigonocephaly). Syndromic forms (Crouzon, Apert, FGFR2 mutations) involve several sutures and risk raised pressure. Positional (deformational) plagiocephaly from supine sleeping gives a parallelogram-shaped head with the ear pushed forward on the flat side, and is managed with repositioning; true lambdoid synostosis pushes the ear backward and gives a trapezoid shape.

title: Scalp layers: birth injuries and scalp wounds
text:
The scalp layers are Skin, dense Connective tissue containing the vessels, the epicranial Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue and Pericranium (SCALP). Vessels in the dense layer are held open by its fibres, so scalp wounds bleed profusely; they are closed in a way that includes the aponeurosis for haemostasis. Wounds through the aponeurosis gape because frontalis and occipitalis pull on it. The loose areolar layer is the 'danger space': infection spreads there and can reach the dural sinuses via valveless emissary veins.
In newborns: caput succedaneum is oedema of the skin and subcutaneous tissue that crosses suture lines and resolves in days. A cephalhaematoma is subperiosteal bleeding, usually over a parietal bone, limited by the sutures because the pericranium is attached there; it may calcify and cause jaundice. A subgaleal haemorrhage beneath the aponeurosis, associated with vacuum delivery, crosses sutures and spreads freely, and can hold a large part of a baby's blood volume, causing shock: a fluctuant boggy scalp with a falling haemoglobin needs urgent resuscitation.

title: Neural tube defects and tethered cord
text:
The neural tube closes by about day 28; failure of the caudal neuropore gives spina bifida and failure of the cranial neuropore gives anencephaly. Spina bifida occulta is a bony defect of the posterior arches with intact skin, often marked by a hair tuft, dimple, haemangioma or lipoma above the natal cleft. A meningocele herniates meninges only; a myelomeningocele also exposes the cord and roots, causing lower limb paralysis and sensory loss at and below the level, neuropathic bladder and bowel, talipes and hip dislocation, and is almost always accompanied by the Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus needing a shunt.
Prevention is folic acid 400 micrograms daily before conception and for the first 12 weeks (5 mg with a previous affected child, diabetes, obesity or antiepileptic drugs; valproate is especially teratogenic). Screening uses raised maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and the anomaly scan (lemon and banana signs).
A tethered cord (conus below L2, fixed by a thick filum or lipoma) is stretched as the child grows, causing back pain, leg weakness, foot deformity, scoliosis and new bladder problems, and is released surgically.

title: Sprengel deformity and Klippel-Feil syndrome
text:
The scapula forms opposite the lower cervical segments and descends to the thorax in weeks 9 to 12. In Sprengel deformity it remains high and small, often joined to the cervical spine by a fibrous or bony omovertebral bar, restricting shoulder abduction and producing a visible asymmetry of the neck line.
It is frequently associated with Klippel-Feil syndrome, a failure of segmentation of cervical vertebrae: the classic triad of a short neck, low posterior hairline and restricted neck movement, although many have only some features. The fused segments concentrate movement at adjacent levels, predisposing to instability, degeneration and cord injury after minor trauma. Associated anomalies include renal agenesis, congenital heart disease, deafness, scoliosis and synkinesis (mirror movements of the hands). Children should have renal ultrasound, audiology and flexion-extension imaging.

title: Pectus excavatum and pectus carinatum
text:
Pectus excavatum (funnel chest), the commonest chest wall deformity, results from overgrowth of the lower costal cartilages pushing the sternum backward; it often becomes more obvious during the adolescent growth spurt. Most concerns are cosmetic and psychological, but severe cases displace and compress the heart, reducing exercise tolerance. It is associated with Marfan and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (check for aortic root dilatation and mitral prolapse). Severity is measured on CT by the Haller index (transverse chest width divided by the sternovertebral distance, above about 3.25 being significant). Correction is by the minimally invasive Nuss procedure, placing a curved steel bar behind the sternum for two to three years, or by open cartilage resection (Ravitch).
Pectus carinatum (pigeon chest) pushes the sternum forward and usually responds to external compression bracing during growth.

title: Atlantoaxial instability
text:
The dens of the axis is held against the anterior arch of the atlas by the transverse ligament, and the atlantodental interval on a lateral radiograph is normally under 3 mm in adults (5 mm in children). Laxity or destruction of the ligament lets C1 slide forward on C2 during flexion, narrowing the canal and compressing the upper cervical cord.
Causes: Down syndrome (ligamentous laxity), rheumatoid arthritis (synovial pannus eroding the ligament and dens; affected patients need cervical spine assessment before anaesthesia and intubation), ankylosing spondylitis, os odontoideum and trauma. Symptoms include neck pain, occipital headache, and upper motor neurone signs: clumsy hands, gait disturbance, hyperreflexia and extensor plantars, and sometimes sudden death. Flexion-extension films or MRI define the instability, and symptomatic cases are fused (C1-C2 posterior fusion).

title: Growth plate (Salter-Harris) fractures
text:
The physis is weaker than the surrounding ligaments and bone in children, so injuries that sprain an adult's joint often fracture a child's growth plate. Salter-Harris classification: I through the physis only (may be invisible on radiograph, tender over the plate); II through the physis and a metaphyseal fragment (commonest, good prognosis); III through the physis and epiphysis into the joint; IV across metaphysis, physis and epiphysis; V a crush of the physis, often recognised only when growth stops ('SALTR': Slipped, Above, Lower, Through, Rammed).
Types III and IV are intra-articular and cross the germinal layer, so they need anatomical reduction, often with fixation, to prevent joint incongruity and a bony bar causing growth arrest, angular deformity or limb-length discrepancy. Distal radius and distal tibia are the common sites. In adolescents whose distal tibial physis is closing from medial to lateral, the Tillaux and triplane fractures occur.

title: Non-accidental injury: skeletal and head signs
text:
Fractures highly specific for abuse include posterior rib fractures near the costovertebral joints (from squeezing the chest, rarely from resuscitation), classic metaphyseal lesions ('corner' and 'bucket handle' fractures from shaking or twisting a limb), scapular, sternal and spinous process fractures, and multiple fractures of different ages. Any fracture in a non-mobile infant, especially a femoral or humeral shaft fracture, needs explanation; a mechanism inconsistent with the child's development, delay in seeking care and a changing story are red flags.
Abusive head trauma in infants causes subdural haematomas of different ages, extensive multilayered retinal haemorrhages and hypoxic brain injury, often with few external signs. Investigation includes a full skeletal survey (repeated after about 11 to 14 days to show healing fractures), CT or MRI of the head, ophthalmology and blood tests to exclude bleeding disorders and bone disease (osteogenesis imperfecta, rickets). Safeguarding procedures are started whenever there is concern.
